prices.name: Lithium carbonate
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Li2CO3 · 99.5% min. Battery-grade threshold; hydroxide route (LiOH·H2O) preferred for high-nickel cathodes.
prices.economic_note: More than doubled from the Jun-2025 ~$8,100/t trough on supply discipline and EV/storage demand. IEA: prices >2x year-ago.

prices.name: Lithium hydroxide
prices.chemistry_key_fact: LiOH·H2O; required for NMC/NCA high-nickel cathodes (low calcination temp, no Li2O loss).
prices.economic_note: Tracks carbonate with a grade premium; supply constrained by conversion capacity outside China.

prices.name: Cobalt
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Co metal 99.8%; sulfate CoSO4·7H2O is the battery intermediate; DRC quota system tightens supply.
prices.economic_note: Recovered from ~$24,300/t (2025) on DRC export quota tightening; CME reports >$25/lb intra-2026. Wide reporting range — treat with caution.

prices.name: Nickel
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Class I (>99.8% Ni) for NMC cathodes; HPAL laterite route (Ni0.8Co0.1Mn0.1(OH)2 precursor).
prices.economic_note: Indonesian laterite oversupply caps prices; Western Class I premium persists for battery use.

prices.name: Copper
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Cu cathode 99.99% (Grade A); 60-70 kg per EV; data-centre and grid demand compounding.
prices.economic_note: Structural deficit consensus (2025-2028); UBS AI/grid thesis cites ~$14,000/t by Sep-2026.

prices.name: Aluminium
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Primary Al via Bayer+Halls-Heroult; 13-16 MWh/t embodied energy — power cost is the price floor.
prices.economic_note: Grid/electrification demand vs Chinese smelting cap; scrap/EAF adjacency for construction materials.

prices.name: Zinc
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Zn 99.995% SHG; galvanising = ~50% of demand; also in zinc-air storage R&D.
prices.economic_note: Construction/steel adjacency; mine closures tightening concentrate supply.

prices.name: Lead
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Pb 99.97%; lead-acid dominance in ESS backup and automotive; 90%+ recycling rate.
prices.economic_note: Stationary storage backup + grid resilience driving secondary Pb demand.

prices.name: Tin
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Sn 99.85%; solders for semiconductors; Myanmar/Indonesia supply concentration.
prices.economic_note: Semiconductor + AI hardware demand; low exchange inventories.

prices.name: Uranium (U3O8)
prices.chemistry_key_fact: U3O8; enrichment to UO2 fuel; SMR/gigawatt-scale buildout extends demand curve.
prices.economic_note: Supply squeeze narrative intact; long-term contracting underpins price floor.

prices.name: Graphite (natural, battery-grade)
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Spherical coated graphite 99.95%C anode; China ~90% of spherical processing.
prices.economic_note: Anode demand growth with EV + ESS; China export-control licensing risk premium.

prices.name: Manganese sulphate
prices.chemistry_key_fact: MnSO4·H2O for LMFP/NMC; China ~95% of battery-grade Mn processing.
prices.economic_note: LMFP adoption lifts demand; processing bottleneck outside China.

prices.name: Neodymium-praseodymium oxide
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Nd2O3/Pr6O11 feed for Nd-Fe-B magnets; administered pricing — not a free-market LME-type price.
prices.economic_note: China domestic vs ex-China dual price regime; magnet demand (EV/wind/defence) structural.

prices.name: Dysprosium oxide
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Dy2O3; ~6.9x China/ex-China multiple (Jul-2026); indispensable for high-temp magnet coercivity.
prices.economic_note: DUAL PRICE: China domestic ~$520k/t vs ex-China ~$3.6M/t. ITAR/NDAA 2027 deadline drives Western premium.

prices.name: Gallium
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Ga 99.99%; GaAs/GaN semiconductors; by-product of alumina refining (no dedicated mines).
prices.economic_note: 2023 export controls reshaped pricing; Chinese quota + foreign-origin licensing.

prices.name: Germanium
prices.chemistry_key_fact: Ge 99.999%; infrared optics, fibre, PV; by-product of zinc/coal fly-ash.
prices.economic_note: Chinese export licensing; defence/IR demand supports premium.

ai_articles.headline: Daily market overview: the composite tells a sharper story than any single print
ai_articles.summary: Across the assessed complex, markets are repricing policy risk faster than physical balance; dated, sourced assessments remain the only durable anchor.
ai_articles.body:
Today's assessment file covers Lithium carbonate, Lithium hydroxide, Cobalt, Nickel, Copper, and the composite picture is more instructive than any single print. The day's notable moves: Dysprosium oxide 3.8% higher; Cobalt 3.2% higher; Neodymium-praseodymium oxide 2.4% higher. Across the complex, the pattern is consistent: markets are repricing policy risk faster than they are repricing physical balance.

The discipline that matters for institutional readers is source integrity. Each figure in the table carries an assessment date (2026-07-22) and a named source, and the reliability tag distinguishes live exchange/FRED prints from assessed baselines that await a live feed. Where no verifiable price exists, the correct notation is GAP — an absence stated plainly, rather than an estimate dressed as data.

The trading implication is structural rather than directional. With processing capacity remaining the binding constraint across lithium, rare earths, graphite and nickel, and with policy calendars running to specific dates, the durable edge belongs to contracts anchored to dated, sourced assessments — not to price forecasts.

Key Takeaway: In this complex, security is a processing question wearing a mining costume. Finance the midstream.

ai_articles.headline: Dysprosium Oxide: the assessment tells a quieter story than the headline
ai_articles.summary: Dysprosium Oxide assessed at 520000 USD/t, 3.8% higher on the day; the structure beneath the print matters more than the move itself.
ai_articles.body:
The numbers in today's data file tell a story that the headlines only gesture at: dysprosium oxide at 520000 USD/t.

Dy2O3; ~6.9x China/ex-China multiple (Jul-2026); indispensable for high-temp magnet coercivity.



On an assessed basis of 520000 USD/t, the move of 3.8% on the day embeds not just physical balance but the market's view of policy risk, inventory behaviour and the financing cost of holding material. The assessment date, 2026-07-15, and its source, Assessed (CREIA / trade monitors), should accompany any institutional citation of this number. The assessment range of 480000 to 560000 USD/t frames the day's print: the low end represents committed tonnage from integrated producers, while the high end is the marginal cost of the last buyer in the market. The location of the print within that band is itself a signal of where the market believes the cycle sits.

The traded form — Dy2O3, China domestic / ex-China — carries its own premium ladder: purity thresholds separate battery grade from technical grade, and the spread between them widens when downstream chemistry becomes the binding constraint. Institutions comparing prices across forms are, in effect, comparing different products.

The supply chain's binding constraint is processing, not geology.

The policy dimension compounds the commercial one. Export licensing, administered pricing and procurement rules all act on this market simultaneously, and each carries a different effective date. The result is a market in which the price is the last thing to move and the first thing to be quoted.

The watch items are therefore concrete: weekly assessment prints from the primary assessors, the spread between administered and assessed quotations, permit decisions on new processing capacity, offtake announcements from the refining stage. Institutions that position against those markers — rather than against the headline number — are the ones whose risk is priced.

For the value chain, the operational translation is direct: buyers who anchor contracts to the structure described above — indexed to a dated assessment with a defined form and purity — convert a volatile commodity into a manageable procurement line. Those who trade headline levels are, in effect, writing optionality on policy they do not control.

Key Takeaway: When a market is administered, a quoted price is a policy signal. When it is assessed, it is a scarcity signal. Know which you are reading.
